info: Takahiro Shindo. Shitao and Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu
statement: A landmark 1988 study by Japanese art historian Takahiro Shindo that interprets Shitao’s Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu as an imaginative reconstruction grounded in past travel rather than a direct topographical record, and as a late masterpiece embodying Shitao’s highly individual method.

info: Lu Fusheng. Duo Yun
statement: Duo Yun was an authoritative academic periodical on Chinese painting founded in 1981 by Shanghai Calligraphy and Painting Publishing House. Under Lu Fusheng it developed into a high-level themed journal and became an important platform for research on Shitao, Dong Qichang, literati painting, and related topics.

info: James Cahill. The Compelling Image: Nature and Style in Seventeenth-Century Chinese Painting
statement: An influential study by James Cahill that treats seventeenth-century Chinese painting as a major moment of creativity, examining the tension between natural representation and stylistic invention and discussing artists such as Zhang Hong, Dong Qichang, Shitao, and Wang Yuanqi.

info: Jonathan Hay. Shitao: Painting and Modernity in Early Qing China
statement: Jonathan Hay’s major monograph on Shitao, first published in English in 2001, widely regarded as the first book-length Western study devoted specifically to Shitao.

info: Yu Huoxing. Re-reading Shitao’s Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu
statement: An article arguing, through inscriptions, Mount Lu topography, and visual analysis, that Shitao’s Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu is a landscape grounded in firsthand travel and poetic tradition rather than a purely conceptual inner landscape.

info: Jeong Seok-do. Daoist Ecological Aesthetics in East Asian Traditional Painting
statement: An article published in 2016 that interprets Shitao’s Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu through Laozi and Daoist ecological aesthetics.

info: Gao Ming
statement: Professor at Shaanxi Normal University whose research in Chinese art history, religious art history, and art education provides important scholarly support for studying the intellectual sources of Shitao’s thought.

info: Li Jianfeng. Integrity, Poeticity, and Worldliness: Chen Hongshou, Shitao, and Tao Yuanming Painting in the Qing
statement: An article arguing that Qing depictions of Tao Yuanming surpassed earlier periods in both quantity and quality, with Chen Hongshou, Dai Benxiao, and Shitao as representative figures.

info: Jiang Deliang, sobriquet Qiushi
statement: Jiang Deliang (1752–1793) was a major Qing scholar, jinshi laureate, epigrapher, collector, calligrapher, painter, and seal carver whose family collection is important for the transmission history of Shitao works.

info: Zhang Changhong. Family Collecting and Its End
statement: A study of the circulation history of the Baiyang–Shitao Calligraphy and Painting Album that reconstructs the collecting lineage of the Jiang family of Yizheng across three generations.

info: Yang Xin, ed. Paintings of the Four Monks
statement: A major Palace Museum catalogue published in 2000 that systematically presents works by Hongren, Kun Can, Bada Shanren, and Shitao, and serves as a core reference on the Four Monks of the early Qing.

info: Wang Shiqing. Recorded Poems of Shitao
statement: A major collected and annotated edition of Shitao’s poems, published in 2006, including 465 poems together with chronology and biographical materials.

info: Shitao. Collected Inscriptions and Colophons on Paintings of Dadi Zi, compiled by Wang Yichen
statement: A manuscript compilation completed in 1732, regarded as the earliest and most original posthumous collection of Shitao’s painting inscriptions and colophons.

info: Shitao, Painting and Calligraphy Combined
statement: In art history and auction records, 'painting and calligraphy combined' refers to a format in which calligraphy and painting are mounted together in the same handscroll or album; Shitao has several extant works of this type.

info: Tian Lin, style name Zhishan, sobriquet Rannong
statement: A Qing figure from Jiangning renowned for seal script, poetry, and seal carving, and an important poetic and artistic friend of Shitao during his Nanjing period.

info: Dong Qichang. Rongtai Bieji, juan 4
statement: A key source for Dong Qichang’s theories of literati painting, collecting, and connoisseurship, especially ideas such as the Southern and Northern schools and the primacy of brushwork and spirit-resonance.

info: Jin Yuan. Shibaizhai Shuhu Lu
statement: An eighteenth-century private catalogue of calligraphy and painting collections that records works, colophons, seals, sizes, and materials, making it a major source for Qing collecting history.

info: Shitao. Collected Notes of the Old Man of Qingxiang
statement: An important engraved Qing compilation of Shitao’s painting inscriptions, poems, and colophons, first printed in 1883 and expanded with an appendix including the sayings of Bitter Gourd Monk.

info: Zhu Liangzhi. Studies on Shitao
statement: A systematic modern study of Shitao that reexamines core concepts of his painting theory, versions of the Huayu Lu, authenticity issues, his relation to Chan and Daoism, and his social network.

info: Pan Zhengwei. Continued Record of Calligraphy and Painting from Tingfanlou
statement: A private catalogue published in 1849 that records 121 works with colophons, seals, and prices, valuable for studying Guangdong collecting and the art market in the Qing.

info: Yang Minggang
statement: A researcher at the Chinese National Academy of Arts specializing in Chinese aesthetics, ancient literary theory, and art criticism.

info: Richard Vinograd. Reminiscences of Ch’in-huai
statement: Richard Vinograd’s 1978 article on Shitao and the Nanjing School, published in Archives of Asian Art.

info: Shitao. Huayu Lu, Chapter 8: Mountains and Rivers
statement: A classic late theoretical text by Shitao on landscape painting. Chapter 8 explains the relation between the principles of heaven and earth, the forms of mountains and rivers, and the painter’s brush-and-ink method.

info: Huang Binhong and Deng Shi, eds. Fine Arts Series
statement: A large modern compilation of traditional Chinese art texts that preserves rare writings on painting theory, epigraphy, seal carving, and connoisseurship from the Six Dynasties through the Qing.

info: Xing Zhiqiang
statement: Associate professor at the China Academy of Art whose research focuses on Chinese character art and technology, calligraphy concept history, and Hanzi design.

info: Zheng Wei. On Shitao’s Life, Intellectual Development, and Artistic Achievement
statement: A foundational 1962 article by the Shanghai Museum scholar Zheng Wei on Shitao’s life trajectory, changing ideas, and artistic accomplishment.

info: Mi Fu. Record of the Elegant Gathering in the Western Garden
statement: Mi Fu’s famous inscription for Li Gonglin’s Elegant Gathering in the Western Garden, long celebrated as a classic account of literati gathering.

info: Cao Yin
statement: Cao Yin (1658–1712), major official, collector, and writer of the Kangxi era, was one of Shitao’s most important late patrons and close friends.

info: Yang Zhongne
statement: Yang Zhongne (1649–1719), scholar-official and compiler associated with Complete Tang Poems, was a core literary friend of both Cao Yin and Shitao.

info: Gu Weizhen
statement: A literatus from Kunshan in the early Qing who maintained close relations with Shitao, Cao Yin, and Wang Zehong.

info: Shitao. Notes of the Old Man of Qingxiang, compiled by Wang Yun
statement: One of the earliest and most authoritative collections of Shitao’s painting poems and inscriptions, often treated together with Collected Inscriptions and Colophons on Paintings of Dadi Zi as a documentary foundation for Shitao studies.

info: Nan Tusheng
statement: An important late Qing collector and editor of art documents who contributed to the preservation and dissemination of materials related to Shitao.

info: Zhang Zining. Hanging Scroll of Ancient Trees Casting Shade by Shitao
statement: A specialized study of Shitao’s Ancient Trees Casting Shade that examines dating, transmission, brushwork, composition, and inscriptions.

info: Zhang Yanyuan. Record of Famous Paintings Through the Ages
statement: The earliest comprehensive Chinese history of painting, completed in 847, and a foundational text for Chinese art history and painting theory.

info: Zhang Daqian. Dafengtang Record of Calligraphy and Painting
statement: An important Republican-era catalogue of Zhang Daqian’s own collection, recording titles, materials, sizes, inscriptions, colophons, and seals.

info: Mei Qing. Later Collection from Tianyan Pavilion
statement: A late chronological poetry collection by Mei Qing, leader of the Xuancheng school, covering works from 1674 to 1688.

info: Series of Titles Listed in the Siku Quanshu Catalogue
statement: A large modern reprint project that gathers books listed in the Siku Quanshu catalogue but not included in the main imperial collection.

info: Li Lin. Collected Writings from Qiufeng
statement: A collection of writings by Li Lin, a loyalist literatus of the Ming–Qing transition, later banned under the Qianlong literary inquisition and preserved in the Siku Banned and Destroyed Books series.

info: Series of Siku Banned and Destroyed Books
statement: A modern facsimile series reprinting rare books that were banned or destroyed during the compilation of the Siku Quanshu.

info: Inscribed Poems on Shitao’s Landscape Album (Ten Leaves), Palace Museum
statement: A late Shitao album in ink on paper, now in the Palace Museum, in which poetry, calligraphy, painting, and seals are closely integrated.

info: Huang Peng
statement: A researcher at the Jiangsu Traditional Chinese Painting Institute known for work on Ming–Qing painting history, collecting history, and art documents, especially Suzhou collecting culture.

info: Kong Shangren. Huhai Ji
statement: A thirteen-juan literary collection by Kong Shangren containing works written during hydraulic engineering service in the Huaiyang coastal region between 1686 and 1689.

info: Yang Xin. Distinguishing the False from the True and Restoring History
statement: A 2008 article reexamining paintings attributed to Qiu Ying of the Elegant Gathering in the Western Garden and arguing for a more complex transmission history behind the image and its textual record.

info: He Fuzheng. Anthology of Distinctions in Literary Forms
statement: A vast Ming anthology and study of literary forms, arranged by genre and intended to supplement earlier classifications of prose and writing.

info: Photolithographic Reprint of the Wenyuan Pavilion Siku Quanshu
statement: The standard Taiwan facsimile edition of the Wenyuan Pavilion copy of the Siku Quanshu, published between 1983 and 1986.

info: Dai Zhuobin
statement: A professional curator at the Shanghai Museum specializing in Ming and Qing painting and calligraphy, conservation, and collecting history.

info: Qin Zuyong. Tongyin Lunhua
statement: An important Qing treatise on painting criticism that evaluates more than 360 painters from the late Ming to the Daoguang era using the four grades of untrammeled, divine, marvelous, and competent.

info: Supplement to the Siku Quanshu
statement: A large 2002 photolithographic series published by Shanghai Ancient Books Publishing House that supplements the original Siku Quanshu with important omitted, banned, or later writings.

info: You Yin, style name Gongfu, sobriquet Shuicun
statement: You Yin (1732–1812), a prominent Yangzhou-school painter and poet of the Qianlong–Jiaqing era, especially known for bamboo painting.

info: Inscriptions and Colophons on Shitao’s Qingxiang Calligraphy-and-Painting Draft, Palace Museum
statement: Qingxiang Calligraphy-and-Painting Draft is a mature long handscroll by Shitao integrating poetry, calligraphy, and painting, compiled from works made for friends and later mounted by the artist himself.

info: Heshen et al. Gazetteer of the Great Qing Unified Realm
statement: A 424-juan official Qing gazetteer completed in 1790 that comprehensively records the empire at the height of the Qianlong era, including territorial expansion and administrative changes.
